newsitem.title: USA: NYC files class action against U.S. auto insurers.
newsitem.headline: NYC files class action against U.S. auto insurers.

text.p: New York City filed a lawsuit Thursday against seven automobile insurers, claiming they overcharged New Yorkers by failing to pass on the savings generated by a dramatic drop in car thefts.

The suit, which seeks class action status and was filed by the city of New York on behalf of the 500,000 New York city residents who hold comprehensive auto insurance, seeks millions of dollars in compensation. The suit was filed in New York State Supreme Court.
It also seeks an injunction ordering the insurers to lower automobile comprehensive insurance rates and premiums.

The suit names Aetna Casualty & Surety Co., Travelers Indemnity Co., Allstate Insurance Co., Government Employees Insurance Co. (GEICO), Liberty Mutual Insurance Co., Nationwide Mutual Insurance Co. and State Farm Fire & Casualty Insurance Co.
In its lawsuit, the city claimed automobile theft in New York dropped to under 60,000 in 1996 from 145,000 in 1990 and continued to decline in 1997.

"Such a massive reduction in automobile theft should have been accompanied by an equally massive reduction in premiums for the type of insurance which covers such losses, automobile comprehensive insurance," the complaint said.
"This is especially true since automobile theft represents nearly 80 percent of the losses paid under such insurance in New York," the complaint said.
However, insurers have failed to appropriately adjust their insurance rates from 1991 to the present, according to the complaint.

But the National Association of Independent Insurers, a non-profit trade group representing more than 565 property-casualty insurance companies, disagreed, saying comprehensive auto insurance rates in New York City have declined along with the city's auto theft rate.
The trade group said State Farm reduced its comprehensive rates in Manhattan 24 percent in 1995 and Nationwide's comprehensive rates fell 21.9 percent in the five boroughs from 1995 to 1996.
GEICO's comprehensive rates fell 19.3 percent from 1988 to 1995 and Allstate's comprehensive rates fell 24 percent on average in New York City's five boroughs since 1991, the trade group said.

"It is important to consider that although theft is a major component of comprehensive coverage, fire, glass, vandalism and weather-related damage all fall under the comprehensive rate as well," said Robert Zeman, vice president and assistant general counsel for the trade group.
The comprehensive coverage is only a small part of the entire insurance premium, explaining why motorists may not be aware of a decline in premium related only to that coverage, the trade group said.
Claims for liability losses in New York continued to rise at a rate as high as 58 percent for Brooklyn furing 1989-1993, the trade group said.
